context.guidance: Serialise only the fields a response needs, using explicit allow-lists or response shapes rather than whole models or nested records. Remove Personal Data Elements the requester is not entitled to see, so each response stays within the Purpose for which the data was collected under §6(1). Apply the same field limits on every route that returns the same record, as Rule 6(1)(b) requires for access control.

value.fix: Don't return the whole `updatedUser` model. Build the response from an explicit allow-list of fields, for example `const { id, name, email, avatarUrl, updatedAt } = updatedUser; res.json({ user: { id, name, email, avatarUrl, updatedAt } })`, or pass it through a shared `toPublicUser(user)` serializer or DTO. Leave out sensitive fields and any the requester isn't entitled to see, such as passwordHash, salt, reset or verification tokens, refresh tokens, MFA secrets, roles or permissions, internal flags, phone, address, date of birth and other personal data unrelated to the profile-update purpose. Don't include nested relations either. Use the same serializer on every route that returns a user record (get profile, list users, login, register, update) so the field limits are the same everywhere. If you use Mongoose or Sequelize, also add schema-level protection: `select: false` or a `toJSON` transform that deletes sensitive fields, or a default scope that excludes them. Add a test that checks the response from this route contains only the allow-listed keys.
